metadata.title: A Short Proof of Bernoulli Disjointness via the Local Lemma

extraction_notes.note: Sections 2 and 4 are proofs without a proof environment that fill their sections; each is one proof node (whole-section exception), so the definition of left D-separated sets and the lemma before the argument in Sec. 4 became steps / nested nodes rather than top-level nodes.
remark or external theorem: Furstenberg's Z-case of Theorem 1.1 is cited by reference only, not stated, so kept as a remark.

nodes.name: Ambient group Gamma
nodes.statement: Throughout, $\Gamma$ denotes an infinite discrete \ep{but not necessarily countable} group.

nodes.name: Hausdorff convention
nodes.statement: All topological spaces in this paper are assumed to be Hausdorff.

nodes.name: Gamma-flow
nodes.statement: A \emphd{$\Gamma$-flow} is a nonempty compact space $X$ equipped with a continuous action $\Gamma \curvearrowright X$.
differentia: equipped with a continuous action $\Gamma \curvearrowright X$

nodes.name: Subflow
nodes.statement: A \emphd{subflow} of a $\Gamma$-flow $X$ is a nonempty closed $\Gamma$-invariant subset $Y \subseteq X$.

nodes.name: Minimal flow
nodes.statement: A $\Gamma$-flow $X$ is \emphd{minimal} if there is no subflow $Y \subseteq X$ with $Y \neq X$; equivalently, $X$ is minimal if the orbit of every point $x \in X$ is dense in $X$.
differentia: there is no subflow $Y \subseteq X$ with $Y \neq X$

nodes.name: Existence of minimal subflows (Zorn)
nodes.statement: A straightforward application of Zorn's lemma shows that every $\Gamma$-flow has a minimal subflow.

nodes.name: Shift action on X^Gamma
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a nonempty compact space. The space $X^\Gamma$ of all functions $\Gamma\to X$, equipped with the product topology, is also compact, and it becomes a $\Gamma$-flow under the action $\Gamma \curvearrowright X^\Gamma$ given by \[ (\gamma \cdot x)(\delta) \,\coloneqq\, x(\delta\gamma) \qquad \text{for all $\gamma$, $\delta \in \Gamma$ and $x \in X^\Gamma$}. \]
nodes.statement_short: $X^\Gamma$ with product topology is a $\Gamma$-flow under right-translation $(\gamma\cdot x)(\delta)=x(\delta\gamma)$.

nodes.name: Bernoulli shift
nodes.statement: The $\Gamma$-flows of the form $X^\Gamma$ are called \emphd{Bernoulli shifts}, or simply \emphd{shifts}.

nodes.name: Finite alphabet k
nodes.statement: A particularly important case is when $X$ is a finite set with the discrete topology; for concreteness, we may then assume that $X = k$ for some $k \in {\mathbb{N}}$.

nodes.name: Natural number as a set
nodes.statement: \ep{Here we identify each $k \in {\mathbb{N}}$ with the $k$-element set $\set{i \in {\mathbb{N}} \,:\, i < k}$.}

nodes.name: Diagonal action on product flow
nodes.statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be $\Gamma$-flows. We view the product space $X \times Y$ as a $\Gamma$-flow equipped with the diagonal action of $\Gamma$.

nodes.name: Joining
nodes.statement: A \emphd{joining} of $X$ and $Y$ is a subflow $Z \subseteq X \times Y$ that projects onto $X$ and $Y$.

nodes.name: Disjointness of flows
nodes.statement: The $\Gamma$-flows $X$ and $Y$ are \emphd{disjoint}, in symbols $X \perp Y$, if they have only one joining, namely $X \times Y$ itself.
differentia: they have only one joining, namely $X \times Y$ itself

nodes.name: Disjoint flows: one is minimal
nodes.statement: It is not hard to see that if $X \perp Y$, then at least one of $X$ and $Y$ is minimal.
conclusions: at least one of $X$ and $Y$ is minimal

nodes.name: Bernoulli disjointness (Glasner-Tsankov-Weiss-Zucker)
nodes.statement: If $X$ is a minimal $\Gamma$-flow, then $X \perp 2^\Gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: Every minimal $\Gamma$-flow is disjoint from the Bernoulli shift $2^\Gamma$.
nodes.label: theo:disj

nodes.name: Furstenberg's case Gamma = Z
nodes.statement: For $\Gamma = \mathbb{Z}$, Theorem~\ref{theo:disj} was proven earlier by Furstenberg \cite{Furstenberg}.

nodes.name: Trapping a point
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a $\Gamma$-flow. We say that a set $U \subseteq X$ \emphd{traps} a point $x \in X$ \ep{or that $x$ is \emphd{trapped} in $U$} if the orbit of $x$ is contained in $U$.
nodes.statement_short: $U$ traps $x$ if the whole orbit of $x$ lies in $U$.

nodes.name: Trapping theorem for finite translates of open sets in k^Gamma
nodes.statement: Let $k \in {\mathbb{N}}^+$ and let $V \subseteq k^\Gamma$ be a nonempty open set. Then there exists $n \in {\mathbb{N}}$ such that for all finite $F \subset \Gamma$ of size at least $n$, the set $F \cdot V$ traps a point.
assumptions: $V \subseteq k^\Gamma$ be a nonempty open set
conclusions: there exists $n \in {\mathbb{N}}$ such that for all finite $F \subset \Gamma$ of size at least $n$, the set $F \cdot V$ traps a point
nodes.statement_short: For nonempty open $V\subseteq k^\Gamma$, every large enough finite set of translates $F\cdot V$ contains a whole orbit.
nodes.label: theo:synd

nodes.name: Derivation of Bernoulli disjointness from the trapping theorem
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a minimal $\Gamma$-flow and let $Z \subseteq X \times 2^\Gamma$ be a joining. Our goal is to show that $Z = X \times 2^\Gamma$. To this end, let $U \subseteq X$ and $V \subseteq 2^\Gamma$ be nonempty open sets. We have to argue that $Z \cap (U \times V) \neq \varnothing$. \begin{lemma} If $X$ is a minimal $\Gamma$-flow and $U \subseteq X$ is a nonempty open set, then there exists an infinite subset $S \subseteq \Gamma$ with $\bigcap \set{\sigma \cdot U \,:\, \sigma \in S} \neq \varnothing$. \end{lemma} \begin{scproof} Since $X$ is minimal, the orbit of each point in $X$ intersects $U$, and thus $X = \Gamma \cdot U$. The compactness of $X$ implies that there is a finite subset $T \subset \Gamma$ such that $X = T \cdot U$. Say that a set $L \subseteq \Gamma$ is \emphd{right $T$-separated} if $\lambda_1T \cap \lambda_2T = \varnothing$ for every pair of distinct $\lambda_1$, $\lambda_2 \in L$. Since $T$ is finite while $\Gamma$ is infinite, there is an infinite right $T$-separated subset $L \subseteq \Gamma$. Consider any $x \in U$. For each $\lambda \in L$, we have $\lambda^{-1} \cdot x \in T \cdot U$, i.e., $x \in \lambda T \cdot U$. In other words, for each $\lambda \in L$, there is $\tau_\lambda \in T$ with $x \in \lambda \tau_\lambda \cdot U$. Since $L$ is right $T$-separated, the set $S \coloneqq \set{\lambda \tau_\lambda \,:\, \lambda \in L}$ is infinite, and we are done. \end{scproof} Let $S \subseteq \Gamma$ be an infinite set as in Lemma~\ref{lemma:rec} applied to $U$, and let $n \in {\mathbb{N}}$ be the quantity given by Theorem~\ref{theo:synd} applied to $V$. Pick an arbitrary finite subset $F \subset S$ of size at least $n$ and let \[ U^\ast \,\coloneqq\, \bigcap \set{\sigma \cdot U \,:\, \sigma \in F}. \] By the choice of $n$, the set $F \cdot V$ traps a point, say $y$. Since $Z$ projects onto $2^\Gamma$, there is some $x \in X$ with $(x,y) \in Z$. As $X$ is minimal and $U^\ast$ is nonempty open, there is $\gamma \in \Gamma$ with $\gamma \cdot x \in U^\ast$. Since $y$ is trapped in $F \cdot V$, we have $\gamma \cdot y \in F \cdot V$, which means that $\sigma^{-1}\gamma \cdot y \in V$ for some $\sigma \in F$, and since $\gamma \cdot x \in U^\ast$, we also have $\sigma^{-1}\gamma \cdot x \in U$. Therefore, \[ (\sigma^{-1}\gamma \cdot x, \, \sigma^{-1}\gamma \cdot y) \,=\, \sigma^{-1}\gamma \cdot (x,y) \,\in\, Z \cap (U \times V), \] and the proof of Theorem~\ref{theo:disj} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Show a joining $Z$ meets every box $U\times V$: recurrence lemma gives $F$, Theorem 2 gives $y$ trapped in $F\cdot V$, minimality moves a partner $x$ into $\bigcap_{\sigma\in F}\sigma U$.

nodes.name: Recurrence lemma for minimal flows
nodes.statement: If $X$ is a minimal $\Gamma$-flow and $U \subseteq X$ is a nonempty open set, then there exists an infinite subset $S \subseteq \Gamma$ with $\bigcap \set{\sigma \cdot U \,:\, \sigma \in S} \neq \varnothing$.
assumptions: $U \subseteq X$ is a nonempty open set
conclusions: there exists an infinite subset $S \subseteq \Gamma$ with $\bigcap \set{\sigma \cdot U \,:\, \sigma \in S} \neq \varnothing$
nodes.statement_short: A nonempty open set in a minimal flow has infinitely many translates with a common point.
nodes.label: lemma:rec

nodes.name: Proof of the recurrence lemma
nodes.statement: Since $X$ is minimal, the orbit of each point in $X$ intersects $U$, and thus $X = \Gamma \cdot U$. The compactness of $X$ implies that there is a finite subset $T \subset \Gamma$ such that $X = T \cdot U$. Say that a set $L \subseteq \Gamma$ is \emphd{right $T$-separated} if $\lambda_1T \cap \lambda_2T = \varnothing$ for every pair of distinct $\lambda_1$, $\lambda_2 \in L$. Since $T$ is finite while $\Gamma$ is infinite, there is an infinite right $T$-separated subset $L \subseteq \Gamma$. Consider any $x \in U$. For each $\lambda \in L$, we have $\lambda^{-1} \cdot x \in T \cdot U$, i.e., $x \in \lambda T \cdot U$. In other words, for each $\lambda \in L$, there is $\tau_\lambda \in T$ with $x \in \lambda \tau_\lambda \cdot U$. Since $L$ is right $T$-separated, the set $S \coloneqq \set{\lambda \tau_\lambda \,:\, \lambda \in L}$ is infinite, and we are done.
nodes.statement_short: Compactness gives finite $T$ with $X=T\cdot U$; pick an infinite right $T$-separated $L$ and set $S=\{\lambda\tau_\lambda\}$.

nodes.name: Reduce to meeting open boxes
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a minimal $\Gamma$-flow and let $Z \subseteq X \times 2^\Gamma$ be a joining. Our goal is to show that $Z = X \times 2^\Gamma$. To this end, let $U \subseteq X$ and $V \subseteq 2^\Gamma$ be nonempty open sets. We have to argue that $Z \cap (U \times V) \neq \varnothing$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce $Z = X\times 2^\Gamma$ to $Z$ meeting every open box $U\times V$.

nodes.name: Recurrence lemma and its proof
nodes.statement: \begin{lemma} If $X$ is a minimal $\Gamma$-flow and $U \subseteq X$ is a nonempty open set, then there exists an infinite subset $S \subseteq \Gamma$ with $\bigcap \set{\sigma \cdot U \,:\, \sigma \in S} \neq \varnothing$. \end{lemma} \begin{scproof} Since $X$ is minimal, the orbit of each point in $X$ intersects $U$, and thus $X = \Gamma \cdot U$. The compactness of $X$ implies that there is a finite subset $T \subset \Gamma$ such that $X = T \cdot U$. Say that a set $L \subseteq \Gamma$ is \emphd{right $T$-separated} if $\lambda_1T \cap \lambda_2T = \varnothing$ for every pair of distinct $\lambda_1$, $\lambda_2 \in L$. Since $T$ is finite while $\Gamma$ is infinite, there is an infinite right $T$-separated subset $L \subseteq \Gamma$. Consider any $x \in U$. For each $\lambda \in L$, we have $\lambda^{-1} \cdot x \in T \cdot U$, i.e., $x \in \lambda T \cdot U$. In other words, for each $\lambda \in L$, there is $\tau_\lambda \in T$ with $x \in \lambda \tau_\lambda \cdot U$. Since $L$ is right $T$-separated, the set $S \coloneqq \set{\lambda \tau_\lambda \,:\, \lambda \in L}$ is infinite, and we are done. \end{scproof}
nodes.statement_short: Inner recurrence lemma with its proof.

nodes.name: Choose S, n, F and U*
nodes.statement: Let $S \subseteq \Gamma$ be an infinite set as in Lemma~\ref{lemma:rec} applied to $U$, and let $n \in {\mathbb{N}}$ be the quantity given by Theorem~\ref{theo:synd} applied to $V$. Pick an arbitrary finite subset $F \subset S$ of size at least $n$ and let \[ U^\ast \,\coloneqq\, \bigcap \set{\sigma \cdot U \,:\, \sigma \in F}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 2.1 and Theorem 1.2 to get $S$, $n$, a finite $F\subset S$ and $U^\ast$.

nodes.name: Trapped point y
nodes.statement: By the choice of $n$, the set $F \cdot V$ traps a point, say $y$.
nodes.statement_short: By the choice of $n$, $F\cdot V$ traps some $y$.

nodes.name: Partner x of y in Z
nodes.statement: Since $Z$ projects onto $2^\Gamma$, there is some $x \in X$ with $(x,y) \in Z$.
nodes.statement_short: Projection of $Z$ gives $x$ with $(x,y)\in Z$.

nodes.name: Move x into U*
nodes.statement: As $X$ is minimal and $U^\ast$ is nonempty open, there is $\gamma \in \Gamma$ with $\gamma \cdot x \in U^\ast$.
nodes.statement_short: Minimality gives $\gamma$ with $\gamma\cdot x\in U^\ast$.

nodes.name: Find sigma
nodes.statement: Since $y$ is trapped in $F \cdot V$, we have $\gamma \cdot y \in F \cdot V$, which means that $\sigma^{-1}\gamma \cdot y \in V$ for some $\sigma \in F$, and since $\gamma \cdot x \in U^\ast$, we also have $\sigma^{-1}\gamma \cdot x \in U$.
nodes.statement_short: Trapping gives $\sigma\in F$ with $\sigma^{-1}\gamma y\in V$ and $\sigma^{-1}\gamma x\in U$.

nodes.name: Conclude Z meets U x V
nodes.statement: Therefore, \[ (\sigma^{-1}\gamma \cdot x, \, \sigma^{-1}\gamma \cdot y) \,=\, \sigma^{-1}\gamma \cdot (x,y) \,\in\, Z \cap (U \times V), \] and the proof of Theorem~\ref{theo:disj} is complete.
nodes.statement_short: The translate of $(x,y)$ lies in $Z\cap(U\times V)$.

nodes.name: X = Gamma U
nodes.statement: Since $X$ is minimal, the orbit of each point in $X$ intersects $U$, and thus $X = \Gamma \cdot U$.
nodes.statement_short: Minimality: translates of $U$ cover $X$.

nodes.name: Finite cover
nodes.statement: The compactness of $X$ implies that there is a finite subset $T \subset \Gamma$ such that $X = T \cdot U$.
nodes.statement_short: Compactness gives a finite $T$ with $X=T\cdot U$.

nodes.name: Infinite right T-separated set
nodes.statement: Say that a set $L \subseteq \Gamma$ is \emphd{right $T$-separated} if $\lambda_1T \cap \lambda_2T = \varnothing$ for every pair of distinct $\lambda_1$, $\lambda_2 \in L$. Since $T$ is finite while $\Gamma$ is infinite, there is an infinite right $T$-separated subset $L \subseteq \Gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: Define right $T$-separated sets and take an infinite one $L$.

nodes.name: Choose tau_lambda
nodes.statement: Consider any $x \in U$. For each $\lambda \in L$, we have $\lambda^{-1} \cdot x \in T \cdot U$, i.e., $x \in \lambda T \cdot U$. In other words, for each $\lambda \in L$, there is $\tau_\lambda \in T$ with $x \in \lambda \tau_\lambda \cdot U$.
nodes.statement_short: For $x\in U$ and each $\lambda\in L$ pick $\tau_\lambda\in T$ with $x\in\lambda\tau_\lambda U$.

nodes.name: S is infinite
nodes.statement: Since $L$ is right $T$-separated, the set $S \coloneqq \set{\lambda \tau_\lambda \,:\, \lambda \in L}$ is infinite, and we are done.
nodes.statement_short: Separation makes $S=\{\lambda\tau_\lambda\}$ infinite.

nodes.name: Bad k-event
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be an arbitrary set and let $k \in {\mathbb{N}}^+$. A \emphd{bad \ep{$k$-}event} over $X$ is a nonempty set $B$ of partial functions $\varphi \colon X \rightharpoonup k$ with finite domains such that for all $\varphi$, $\varphi' \in B$, $\mathrm{dom}(\varphi) = \mathrm{dom}(\varphi')$.
nodes.genus: nonempty set $B$ of partial functions $\varphi \colon X \rightharpoonup k$ with finite domains
nodes.statement_short: A bad event is a nonempty set of finite partial maps $X\rightharpoonup k$ sharing a common domain.

nodes.name: Domain of a bad event
nodes.statement: If a bad event $B$ is nonempty, then its \emphd{domain} is the set $\mathrm{dom}(B) \coloneqq \mathrm{dom}(\varphi)$ for any \ep{hence all} $\varphi \in B$; the domain of the empty bad event is, by definition, the empty set.

nodes.name: Probability of a bad event
nodes.statement: The \emphd{probability} of a bad $k$-event $B$ with domain $D$ is defined to be $\mathbb{P}[B] \coloneqq |B|/k^{|D|}$.

nodes.name: Avoiding a bad event
nodes.statement: A map $f \colon X \to k$ \emphd{avoids} a bad event $B$ if there is no $\varphi \in B$ such that $\varphi \subseteq f$.

nodes.name: Probabilistic meaning of P[B]
nodes.statement: Notice that if $X$ is finite and $f \colon X \to k$ is drawn uniformly at random from $k^X$, then $\mathbb{P}[B]$ is precisely the probability that $f$ \emph{does not} avoid $B$.

nodes.name: Instance of the LLL
nodes.statement: A~\emphd{\ep{$k$\=/}instance \ep{of the LLL}} over a set $X$ is an arbitrary set ${\mathscr{B}}$ of bad $k$-events over $X$.

nodes.name: Solution of an instance
nodes.statement: A~\emphd{solution} to a $k$-instance~${\mathscr{B}}$ is a function $f \colon X \to k$ that avoids every $B \in {\mathscr{B}}$.

nodes.name: Neighborhood of a bad event
nodes.statement: For an instance ${\mathscr{B}}$ and $B \in {\mathscr{B}}$, the \emphd{neighborhood} of $B$ in ${\mathscr{B}}$ is the set \[ \mathrm{N}_{\mathscr{B}}(B) \coloneqq \set{B' \in {\mathscr{B}} \setminus \set{B} \,:\, \mathrm{dom}(B') \cap \mathrm{dom}(B) \neq \varnothing}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Neighborhood of $B$: the other bad events whose domains meet $\mathrm{dom}(B)$.

nodes.name: Degree of a bad event
nodes.statement: The \emphd{degree} of $B$ in ${\mathscr{B}}$ is defined to be $\deg_{\mathscr{B}}(B) \coloneqq |\mathrm{N}_{\mathscr{B}}(B)|$.

nodes.name: Max probability p(B) and max degree d(B)
nodes.statement: Let \[ p({\mathscr{B}}) \coloneqq \sup_{B \in {\mathscr{B}}} \mathbb{P}[B] \qquad \text{and} \qquad d({\mathscr{B}}) \coloneqq \sup_{B \in {\mathscr{B}}} \deg_{\mathscr{B}}(B). \]

nodes.name: Correct instance for the LLL
nodes.statement: An instance ${\mathscr{B}}$ is \emphd{correct for the LLL}, or simply \emphd{correct}, if \[ e\cdot p({\mathscr{B}}) \cdot (d({\mathscr{B}}) + 1) < 1, \] where $e = 2.71\ldots${} denotes the base of the natural logarithm.

nodes.name: Lovász Local Lemma
nodes.statement: Let $k \in {\mathbb{N}}^+$ and let ${\mathscr{B}}$ be a $k$-instance of the LLL over a set $X$. If ${\mathscr{B}}$ is correct for the LLL, then ${\mathscr{B}}$ has a solution.
assumptions: ${\mathscr{B}}$ be a $k$-instance of the LLL over a set $X$
nodes.label: theo:LLL

nodes.name: LLL here is the variable-framework special case
nodes.statement: We should mention that there are two respects in which Theorem~\ref{theo:LLL} in the above form is less general then the ``full'' LLL. First, Theorem~\ref{theo:LLL} only works with \emph{product} probability spaces such as $k^X$; this is a special case of the~LLL in the so-called \emph{variable framework} (the~name is due to Kolipaka and Szegedy~\cite{KolipakaSzegedy}). However, although this case is special, it does encompass most typical applications. For the statement of the~LLL for general probability spaces, see~\cite[Corollary~5.1.2]{AS}.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 3.1 only covers product spaces $k^X$ (the variable framework), which suffices for most applications.

nodes.name: Deduction of the LLL from the general version
nodes.statement: Deducing Theorem~\ref{theo:LLL} from \cite[Corollary~5.1.2]{AS} is routine when $X$ is finite (see, e.g., \cite[41]{MR}); the case of infinite~$X$ then follows by compactness.
nodes.statement_short: Routine reduction to the general LLL [AS, Cor. 5.1.2] for finite $X$, then compactness for infinite $X$.

nodes.name: General Lovasz Local Lemma not needed
nodes.statement: Second, there is a more general form of the LLL \ep{often referred to as the \emph{General Lov\'asz Local Lemma}}, that applies to instances without a uniform upper bound on $\deg_{\mathscr{B}}(B)$; see \cite[Theorem 5.1.1]{AS}. However, this more general statement is somewhat technical and we will not need it here.

nodes.name: Proof of the trapping theorem via the LLL
nodes.statement_short: Lovász Local Lemma on bad events $B_\gamma$ over $k^\Gamma$ indexed by $\gamma$. A solution is trapped in $L\cdot V_\varphi$ for a left $D$-separated $L^{-1}$; degree $\le |D|^2|L|^2-1$ and probability $(1-k^{-|D|})^{|L|}$ make it correct.

nodes.name: Large left D-separated subsets
nodes.statement: If $D$, $F \subset \Gamma$ are finite sets, then $F$ has a left $D$-separated subset $L \subseteq F$ with \[|L| \geqslant |F|/|D|^2.\]
conclusions: $F$ has a left $D$-separated subset $L \subseteq F$ with \[|L| \geqslant |F|/|D|^2.\]
nodes.label: lemma:indep

nodes.name: Proof of the separated-subset lemma
nodes.statement: First recall some basic facts about finite graphs. Let $G$ be a finite graph with vertex set $V$ and edge set $E$. A subset $I \subseteq V$ is \emphd{independent \ep{in $G$}} if no two vertices in $I$ are adjacent to each other. A straightforward greedy construction shows that if every vertex of $G$ has at most $d$ neighbors, then $V$ can be partitioned into $d+1$ independent sets. In particular, $G$ has an independent set of size at least $|V|/(d+1)$. Now let $G$ be the graph with vertex set $F$ in which distinct vertices $\sigma$, $\sigma' \in F$ are adjacent if and only if $D\sigma \cap D\sigma' \neq \varnothing$, or, equivalently, $\sigma' \in D^{-1}D\sigma$. Every $\sigma \in F$ has at most $|D^{-1}D| - 1 \leqslant |D|^2 - 1$ neighbors in $G$ \ep{we are subtracting $1$ to account for the fact that $\sigma$ is not adjacent to itself}. Therefore, $G$ has an independent set $L$ of size at least $|F|/|D|^2$, and that is precisely what we need.
nodes.statement_short: Greedy independent-set bound in the graph on $F$ joining $\sigma,\sigma'$ when $D\sigma\cap D\sigma'\neq\varnothing$, of max degree $<|D|^2$.

nodes.name: Choice of ell_0
nodes.statement: e \cdot (1 - k^{-|D|})^\ell \cdot |D|^2\ell^2 \,<\, 1 \qquad \text{for all } \ell \geqslant \ell_0.
nodes.statement_short: $\ell_0$ chosen so that $e(1-k^{-|D|})^\ell |D|^2\ell^2<1$ for all $\ell\ge\ell_0$.
nodes.label: eq:endgame

nodes.name: Recall greedy independent sets
nodes.statement: First recall some basic facts about finite graphs. Let $G$ be a finite graph with vertex set $V$ and edge set $E$. A subset $I \subseteq V$ is \emphd{independent \ep{in $G$}} if no two vertices in $I$ are adjacent to each other. A straightforward greedy construction shows that if every vertex of $G$ has at most $d$ neighbors, then $V$ can be partitioned into $d+1$ independent sets. In particular, $G$ has an independent set of size at least $|V|/(d+1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall that a graph of max degree $d$ has an independent set of size $\ge |V|/(d+1)$.

nodes.name: Apply to the overlap graph on F
nodes.statement: Now let $G$ be the graph with vertex set $F$ in which distinct vertices $\sigma$, $\sigma' \in F$ are adjacent if and only if $D\sigma \cap D\sigma' \neq \varnothing$, or, equivalently, $\sigma' \in D^{-1}D\sigma$. Every $\sigma \in F$ has at most $|D^{-1}D| - 1 \leqslant |D|^2 - 1$ neighbors in $G$ \ep{we are subtracting $1$ to account for the fact that $\sigma$ is not adjacent to itself}. Therefore, $G$ has an independent set $L$ of size at least $|F|/|D|^2$, and that is precisely what we need.
nodes.statement_short: The overlap graph on $F$ has max degree $\le |D|^2-1$, giving the independent set $L$.

nodes.name: Left D-separated sets
nodes.statement: Let $D \subset \Gamma$ be a finite set. We say that a set $L \subseteq \Gamma$ is \emphd{left $D$-separated} if $D\lambda_1 \cap D\lambda_2 = \varnothing$ for every pair of distinct $\lambda_1$, $\lambda_2 \in L$.
nodes.statement_short: Define left $D$-separated subsets of $\Gamma$.

nodes.name: Separated-subset lemma and its proof
nodes.statement: \begin{lemma} If $D$, $F \subset \Gamma$ are finite sets, then $F$ has a left $D$-separated subset $L \subseteq F$ with \[|L| \geqslant |F|/|D|^2.\] \end{lemma} \begin{scproof} First recall some basic facts about finite graphs. Let $G$ be a finite graph with vertex set $V$ and edge set $E$. A subset $I \subseteq V$ is \emphd{independent \ep{in $G$}} if no two vertices in $I$ are adjacent to each other. A straightforward greedy construction shows that if every vertex of $G$ has at most $d$ neighbors, then $V$ can be partitioned into $d+1$ independent sets. In particular, $G$ has an independent set of size at least $|V|/(d+1)$. Now let $G$ be the graph with vertex set $F$ in which distinct vertices $\sigma$, $\sigma' \in F$ are adjacent if and only if $D\sigma \cap D\sigma' \neq \varnothing$, or, equivalently, $\sigma' \in D^{-1}D\sigma$. Every $\sigma \in F$ has at most $|D^{-1}D| - 1 \leqslant |D|^2 - 1$ neighbors in $G$ \ep{we are subtracting $1$ to account for the fact that $\sigma$ is not adjacent to itself}. Therefore, $G$ has an independent set $L$ of size at least $|F|/|D|^2$, and that is precisely what we need. \end{scproof}
nodes.statement_short: Inner lemma on large left $D$-separated subsets, with its proof.

nodes.name: Cylinder sets V_phi
nodes.statement: For a partial map $\varphi \colon \Gamma \rightharpoonup k$ with finite domain, let $V_\varphi \subseteq k^\Gamma$ denote the clopen set given by \[ V_\varphi \,\coloneqq\, \set{x \in k^\Gamma \,:\, x \supset \varphi}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Define the clopen cylinder $V_\varphi$.

nodes.name: Reduce to cylinder sets
nodes.statement: Since the topology on $k^\Gamma$ is generated by the sets of the form $V_\varphi$, it is enough to prove Theorem~\ref{theo:synd} with $V = V_\varphi$.
nodes.statement_short: Cylinders form a base, so it suffices to treat $V=V_\varphi$.

nodes.name: Fix D, phi, ell_0 and n
nodes.statement: So, let $D \subset \Gamma$ be a nonempty finite set and let $\varphi \colon D \to k$. Let $\ell_0 \in {\mathbb{N}}$ be such that \begin{equation} e \cdot (1 - k^{-|D|})^\ell \cdot |D|^2\ell^2 \,<\, 1 \qquad \text{for all } \ell \geqslant \ell_0. \end{equation} \ep{Such $\ell_0$ exists since the left-hand side of \eqref{eq:endgame} approaches $0$ as $\ell$ goes to infinity.} We shall argue that $n \coloneqq \ell_0|D|^2$ is as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $\varphi:D\to k$, choose $\ell_0$ via (4.1) and set $n=\ell_0|D|^2$.

nodes.name: Separated L inside F
nodes.statement: Take any finite set $F \subset \Gamma$ of size at least $n$ and let $L \subseteq F$ be a set of size at least $|F|/|D|^2 \geqslant \ell_0$ such that $L^{-1}$ is left $D$-separated \ep{such $L$ exists due to Lemma~\ref{lemma:indep} applied with $F^{-1}$ in place of $F$}.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 4.1 applied to $F^{-1}$ gives $L\subseteq F$, $|L|\ge\ell_0$, with $L^{-1}$ left $D$-separated.

nodes.name: Define the LLL instance
nodes.statement: Define a $k$-instance ${\mathscr{B}}$ over $\Gamma$ as follows. For each $\gamma \in \Gamma$, let $B_\gamma$ be the bad $k$-event with domain $D_\gamma \coloneqq D L^{-1}\gamma$ consisting of all maps $\psi \colon D_\gamma \to k$ such that: \[ \text{for each } \lambda \in L,\ \text{there is } \delta \in D\ \text{with } \psi(\delta\lambda^{-1}\gamma) \,\neq\, \varphi(\delta). \] Notice that since $L^{-1}$ is left $D$-separated, $D_\gamma$ is equal to the \emph{disjoint} union of the sets $D \lambda^{-1}\gamma$, $\lambda \in L$. Let ${\mathscr{B}}\coloneqq \set{B_\gamma \,:\, \gamma \in \Gamma}$.
nodes.statement_short: Define bad events $B_\gamma$ with domain $DL^{-1}\gamma$ and the instance $\mathscr{B}$.

nodes.name: Solutions are trapped
nodes.statement: We claim that if $x \colon \Gamma\to k$ is a solution to ${\mathscr{B}}$, then $x$ is trapped in $L \cdot V_\varphi$ \ep{and hence also in $F \cdot V_\varphi$}. Indeed, consider any $\gamma \in \Gamma$. Since $x$ avoids $B_\gamma$, the following holds: \[ \text{there is } \lambda \in L\ \text{such that for all } \delta \in D, \ x(\delta \lambda^{-1}\gamma) \,=\, \varphi(\delta). \] But this precisely means that for some $\lambda \in L$, $\lambda^{-1}\gamma \cdot x \supset \varphi$, i.e., $\gamma \cdot x \in L \cdot V_\varphi$.
nodes.statement_short: Claim: any solution of $\mathscr{B}$ is trapped in $L\cdot V_\varphi$.

nodes.name: Avoiding B_gamma
nodes.statement: Indeed, consider any $\gamma \in \Gamma$. Since $x$ avoids $B_\gamma$, the following holds: \[ \text{there is } \lambda \in L\ \text{such that for all } \delta \in D, \ x(\delta \lambda^{-1}\gamma) \,=\, \varphi(\delta). \]
nodes.statement_short: Avoiding $B_\gamma$ yields $\lambda$ with $x$ matching $\varphi$ on $D\lambda^{-1}\gamma$.

nodes.name: Translate into trapping
nodes.statement: But this precisely means that for some $\lambda \in L$, $\lambda^{-1}\gamma \cdot x \supset \varphi$, i.e., $\gamma \cdot x \in L \cdot V_\varphi$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $\gamma\cdot x\in L\cdot V_\varphi$.

nodes.name: Remains: correctness
nodes.statement: In view of Theorem~\ref{theo:LLL}, it only remains to show that ${\mathscr{B}}$ is correct for the LLL.
nodes.statement_short: By the LLL it remains to check correctness of $\mathscr{B}$.

nodes.name: Degree: set up
nodes.statement: First we bound $d({\mathscr{B}})$. Consider any $\gamma \in \Gamma$. We need to find an upper bound on the size of the set \[ \set{\gamma' \in \Gamma \setminus \set{\gamma} \,:\, D_\gamma \cap D_{\gamma'} \neq \varnothing}. \]
nodes.statement_short: To bound $d(\mathscr{B})$, count the $\gamma'$ with $D_\gamma\cap D_{\gamma'}\neq\varnothing$.

nodes.name: Degree bound
nodes.statement: To this end, notice that $D_\gamma \cap D_{\gamma'} \neq \varnothing$ if and only if $\gamma' \in LD^{-1}DL^{-1}\gamma$. Thus, \[ \left|\set{\gamma' \in \Gamma \setminus \set{\gamma} \,:\, D_\gamma \cap D_{\gamma'} \neq \varnothing}\right| \,=\, |LD^{-1}DL^{-1}| - 1 \,\leqslant\, |D|^2|L|^2 - 1, \] and hence we conclude that $d({\mathscr{B}}) \leqslant |D|^2|L|^2 - 1$.
nodes.statement_short: $d(\mathscr{B})\le|D|^2|L|^2-1$.

nodes.name: Probability bound
nodes.statement: Next we bound $p({\mathscr{B}})$. Again, fix $\gamma \in \Gamma$ and draw $f \colon D_\gamma \to k$ uniformly at random. Then for each $\lambda \in L$, \[ \mathbb{P}[f(\delta \lambda^{-1} \gamma) \neq \varphi(\delta) \text{ for some } \delta \in D] \,=\, 1 - k^{-|D|}, \] and since the sets $D \lambda^{-1}\gamma$, $\lambda \in L$ are disjoint, we conclude that \[ \mathbb{P}[B_\gamma] \,=\, (1 - k^{-|D|})^{|L|}. \] Therefore, $p({\mathscr{B}}) \leqslant (1 - k^{-|D|})^{|L|}$.
nodes.statement_short: By disjointness, $p(\mathscr{B})\le(1-k^{-|D|})^{|L|}$.

nodes.name: Conclude via (4.1)
nodes.statement: To put everything together, ${\mathscr{B}}$ is correct as long as \[ e \cdot (1 - k^{-|D|})^{|L|} \cdot |D|^2|L|^2 \,<\, 1. \] Since $|L| \geqslant \ell_0$, \eqref{eq:endgame} gives the desired result.
nodes.statement_short: Correctness reduces to (4.1) since $|L|\ge\ell_0$.
